name: UX designer
summary: UX design interviews usually centre on your portfolio: candidates commonly report walking through two or three projects and explaining the problem, the research and the decisions behind each design. Many companies add a design exercise (a take-home or a live whiteboard task) and questions on research methods, usability and working with product managers and engineers.
rounds: Recruiter or HR screen, often with a quick look at your portfolio
Portfolio review: present two or three projects and answer questions on them
Design exercise: a take-home or a live task on a product problem
Collaboration round with a product manager or engineer (for some roles)
Hiring manager or design leader round
looks_for: A clear process: problem, research, ideas, testing, decision
Explaining why you made each decision, not just showing final screens
Research that changes the design: interviews, usability tests, data
Accessibility, and consistency through a design system
Taking feedback well and explaining trade-offs
Working within real limits: time, technology and business goals

questions.text: Tell me about a design decision you defended with research when others disagreed.
covers: The disagreement and who was involved
The evidence you used: a usability test, interviews, data
The outcome, and what you'd do the same or differently

questions.text: Describe a time user testing showed that your design wasn't working.
covers: What you expected and what users actually did
How you changed the design
What it taught you about testing earlier

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to design within a strict technical or time limit.
covers: The limit, and what the ideal design would have needed
The compromise you made and how you kept it usable
What shipped, and any follow-up

questions.text: Tell me about feedback on your work that was hard to hear. What did you do with it?
covers: The feedback and your first reaction, honestly
What you did with it
How your work changed as a result

questions.text: Walk me through one project in your portfolio, from the problem to the final design.
covers: The problem, the users and your exact role
The research, the options you explored and why you chose one
The result, and what you learned

questions.text: How would you redesign a shopping app's checkout so fewer people abandon their carts?
covers: Finding where and why people drop off, from data and session recordings
Fixes such as fewer steps, guest checkout, showing all costs early, saved payment details
How you'd test the change and measure it

questions.text: Design a way for patients to book doctor's appointments on their phone. Talk me through your process.
covers: The users and their situations: patients, carers, clinic staff
The key flows: finding a doctor, choosing a slot, reminders, cancelling
Accessibility for older users, and how you'd test a prototype

questions.text: Which research methods do you use, and how do you pick one for a project?
covers: Interviews, usability tests, surveys, analytics and card sorting
Matching the method to the question: why people do something versus how many do it
What you do with little time or budget

questions.text: How do you run a usability test, and how do you avoid influencing the participant?
covers: Tasks based on real goals, worded so they don't give the answer away
Asking people to think aloud, and staying neutral
Turning findings into prioritised changes

questions.text: What makes a design accessible? Name the checks you'd run on a new screen.
covers: Colour contrast, text size, and not relying on colour alone
Labels, focus order and screen reader support
Touch target sizes and plain language

questions.text: What is a design system, and how do you balance using it with designing something new?
covers: Shared components, styles and rules that keep products consistent
When to reuse an existing pattern and when a new one is justified
How you'd propose adding to the system

questions.text: A product manager wants another feature added to a screen that's already crowded. How do you respond?
covers: Understanding the goal behind the request
Options: showing it only when needed, placing it elsewhere, removing something else
Testing with users and agreeing the outcome with the PM

questions.text: How do you hand designs over to engineers so they get built as intended?
covers: Specs covering every state (empty, error, loading), not just the happy path
Using shared components, and talking early about what's hard to build
Reviewing the build together and fixing gaps

questions.text: How would you measure whether a redesign improved the user experience?
covers: Task success, time on task and error rates
Business measures such as conversion or support tickets
User feedback, and comparing before and after fairly

questions.text: What's the difference between UX and UI design, and where do your strengths lie?
covers: UX as the overall experience and flow; UI as the visual and interactive layer
How the two overlap in practice
Your strengths, shown with an example

questions.text: Why UX design? What first made you care about how products feel to use?
covers: A moment or project that drew you in
What you enjoy most: research, interaction design, visual craft
Where you want to grow

questions.text: What's one thing you'd improve about our product's experience?
covers: Evidence that you've used the product
A specific issue, and who it affects
A focused change, and how you'd test it

tips: Pick two or three portfolio projects and tell each as a story: the problem, your role, the research, the decisions, the result.
Show messy work too: sketches, rejected options and test findings show how you think.
In live exercises, ask who the user is and what success means before you draw anything.
Be clear about what you did yourself on team projects; interviewers often ask you to separate your work from the team's.
Have a short version of each case study ready in case the interviewer runs out of time.
If you're a fresher, a self-started project with genuine user testing can stand in for work experience.
